```{r}
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(rsample)
library(yardstick)
library(torch)
library(torchvision)

library(magick)
source("sherd_helpers.R")


```

Step 1: Import the data
The data come from the paper's supplement on Zenodo ( (opens in new tab)https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4625156). We need the spreadsheet of classifications and the folder of 2,407 sherd images.

```{r}
tww_file <- "data/CNN-Models-Supplement/TWW_data.xlsx"
image_dir <- "data/Single_Sherd_8_Type_Analyzer/Reference_Database/Reference_Images"

tww <- read_excel(tww_file)
```

```{r}
type_levels <- c("Kanaa", "Wepo", "Black_Mesa", "Sosi", "Dogoszhi", "Flagstaff", "Tusayan", "Kayenta")

sherds <- tww |>
  transmute(
    image = image_file,
    type = factor(`Human consensus`, levels = type_levels),
    paper_prediction = `CNN model prediction`
  ) |>
  mutate(path = file.path(image_dir, image))

count(sherds, type)
```

```{r}
sample_prop <- 0.25

set.seed(459)
sherd_sample <- sherds |>
  group_by(type) |>
  slice_sample(prop = sample_prop) |>
  ungroup()

count(sherd_sample, type)
```

```{r}
set.seed(459)
sherd_split <- initial_split(sherd_sample, prop = 0.8, strata = type)
train_df <- training(sherd_split)
test_df <- testing(sherd_split)

```

The training set has `r nrow(train_df)` sherds and the test set has `r nrow(test_df)` sherds.

```{r}
train_dl <- dataloader(sherd_dataset(train_df, 
                                     augment = TRUE), 
                       batch_size = 32, 
                       shuffle = TRUE)

test_dl <- dataloader(sherd_dataset(test_df, 
                                    augment = FALSE),
                      batch_size = 64)
```

```{r}
sherd_net <- nn_module(
  initialize = function() {
    self$resnet <- model_resnet18(pretrained = TRUE)
    self$resnet$fc <- nn_linear(512, 8) # fc refers to the Fully Connected layer
  },
  forward = function(x) self$resnet(x)
)
```

```{r}
torch_manual_seed(459)

fitted <- sherd_net |>
  setup(
    loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss(),
    optimizer = optim_adam,
    metrics = luz_metric_accuracy()
  ) |>
  set_opt_hparams(lr = 0.0001) |>
  fit(train_dl, epochs = 15, valid_data = test_dl, verbose = FALSE)
```
```{r}
plot(fitted)
```

```{r}
test_logits <- predict(fitted, test_dl)
test_probs <- as_array(nnf_softmax(test_logits, dim = 2)$cpu())

test_results <- test_df |>
  mutate(predicted = factor(type_levels[max.col(test_probs)], levels = type_levels))

accuracy(test_results, truth = type, estimate = predicted)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-confusion-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix of true versus predicted types for the test sherds"

conf_matrix <- test_results |>
  count(type, predicted, name = "n") |>
  complete(type, predicted, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  mutate(dark = n >= max(n) / 2)

ggplot(conf_matrix, aes(predicted, type)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = n), colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, colour = dark), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Sherds") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey10", "TRUE" = "white"), guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Predicted type", y = "True type") +
  theme_minimal()
```
This figure the true types compared to predicted types, and how many times the model correctly and incorrectly predicted the pottery type. The model had the most trouble classifying Wepo, incorrectly classifying all 3 sherds. It also had trouble with Black Mesa, Flagstadd, Kayenta, and more. Many of the incorrectly predicted sherds fell into types that were nearby in time. However some, specifically Black Mesa, had incorrect predictions all across the time scale. Among the most accurate are Kanaa with 0.8 recall, Sosi with 0.91 recall, and Tusayan with 0.89 recall. Overall, our accuracy (0.,73) is decently high, although much lower than the paper's accuracy (0.89). Our model definitely can predict many sherds types, but still struggles with classifying many sherds and specific types.  

```{r}
comparison <- tibble(
  classifier = c("Our ResNet18", "Paper's CNN ensemble"),
  agreement = c(
    mean(test_results$predicted == test_results$type),
    mean(test_results$paper_prediction == test_results$type)
  )
)

comparison

```


```{r}
recall_by_type <- test_results |>
  summarise(
    n_test = n(),
    recall = mean(predicted == type),
    paper_recall = mean(paper_prediction == type),
    .by = type
  )

precision_by_type <- test_results |>
  summarise(precision = mean(predicted == type), .by = predicted)

recall_by_type |>
  left_join(precision_by_type, by = join_by(type == predicted)) |>
  relocate(precision, .after = n_test) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Is our model's accuracy inside the range of the human analysts? Is that a fair way to judge a CNN?

Our model's accuracy is about 0.73, while the agreement between human analysts was between 0.736–0.869, so ours is at the bottom of their accuracy, slightly below it. This isn't necessarily a fair way to judge a CNN since only four expert analysts were used as comparison, and may get different accuracy every time, while the model should get similar accuracy every time. This also isn't a way to judge any other factors, for example time. An analyst would spend considerable more time looking at pottery than a model would, but could also pick up things that the model may have missed, or provide context that a model could not. 

Which types are confused most often? Are they neighbours in time? What does this suggest about the types themselves (for example Wepo)?

The model wrongly predicted 7 Black Mesa sherds as Sosi, 4 Kayenta sherds were wrongly predicted as Tusayan, and 3 Flagstaff sherds were wrongly predicted as Tusayan. These are the types with the highest numbers of wrongly predicted types, and all wrongly predicted types are neighbors in time with their true types. This suggests that some of these could be transition types, and do not strictly fit into one singular type. For example, the study states that Wepo could be a transition type between Kanaa and Black Mesa, which would explain why it is wrongly predicted as Black Mesa.
